claim: In C. elegans, death-associated protein kinase (DAPK-1) regulates epidermal morphogenesis, innate immunity and wound repair.
source: In C. elegans, death-associated protein kinase (DAPK-1) regulates epidermal morphogenesis, innate immunity and wound repair.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of DAPK-1, supported by prior work referenced in the introduction (Tong et al., 2009).

claim: dapk-1 epidermal phenotypes are suppressed by treatment with microtubule-destabilizing drugs.
source: dapk-1 epidermal phenotypes are suppressed by treatment with microtubule-destabilizing drugs and mimicked or enhanced by microtubule-stabilizing drugs.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with colchicine treatment shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dapk-1 epidermal phenotypes are mimicked or enhanced by microtubule-stabilizing drugs.
source: dapk-1 epidermal phenotypes are suppressed by treatment with microtubule-destabilizing drugs and mimicked or enhanced by microtubule-stabilizing drugs.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with paclitaxel treatment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of function in ptrn-1 suppresses dapk-1 epidermal phenotypes.
source: Loss of function in ptrn-1, the C. elegans member of the Patronin/Nezha/CAMSAP family of MT minus-end binding proteins, suppresses dapk-1 epidermal and innate immunity phenotypes.
evidence: Shown in genetic suppressor screen results presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of function in ptrn-1 suppresses dapk-1 innate immunity phenotypes.
source: Loss of function in ptrn-1, the C. elegans member of the Patronin/Nezha/CAMSAP family of MT minus-end binding proteins, suppresses dapk-1 epidermal and innate immunity phenotypes.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2A,B showing suppression of nlp-29 expression.

claim: Over-expression of the MT-binding CKK domain of PTRN-1 triggers epidermal defects resembling those of dapk-1 mutants.
source: Over-expression of the MT-binding CKK domain of PTRN-1 triggers epidermal and immunity defects resembling those of dapk-1 mutants, and PTRN-1 localization is regulated by DAPK-1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B,C demonstrating that CKK domain expression induces Mor phenotypes.

claim: Over-expression of the MT-binding CKK domain of PTRN-1 triggers immunity defects resembling those of dapk-1 mutants.
source: Over-expression of the MT-binding CKK domain of PTRN-1 triggers epidermal and immunity defects resembling those of dapk-1 mutants, and PTRN-1 localization is regulated by DAPK-1.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5D showing nlp-29 expression induced by CKK domain.

claim: PTRN-1 localization is regulated by DAPK-1.
source: Over-expression of the MT-binding CKK domain of PTRN-1 triggers epidermal and immunity defects resembling those of dapk-1 mutants, and PTRN-1 localization is regulated by DAPK-1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A-E demonstrating increased PTRN-1 filaments in dapk-1(ju4) mutants.

claim: DAPK-1 and PTRN-1 physically interact in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: DAPK-1 and PTRN-1 physically interact in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, and DAPK-1 itself undergoes MT-dependent transport.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing co-IP results in HEK293T cells.

claim: DAPK-1 undergoes MT-dependent transport.
source: DAPK-1 and PTRN-1 physically interact in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, and DAPK-1 itself undergoes MT-dependent transport.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7A-E demonstrating GFP::DAPK-1 puncta movement that is reduced by colchicine treatment.

claim: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in stress responses.
source: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in stress responses (Tu et al., 2010), antiviral immunity (Zhang et al.), and in IL-1ß-associated inflammatory diseases (Chakilam et al., 2013; Chuang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2010.

claim: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in antiviral immunity.
source: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in stress responses (Tu et al., 2010), antiviral immunity (Zhang et al.), and in IL-1ß-associated inflammatory diseases (Chakilam et al., 2013; Chuang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al.

claim: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in IL-1ß-associated inflammatory diseases.
source: Mammalian DAPK1 has been implicated in stress responses (Tu et al., 2010), antiviral immunity (Zhang et al.), and in IL-1ß-associated inflammatory diseases (Chakilam et al., 2013; Chuang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chakilam et al., 2013 and Chuang et al., 2011.

claim: DAPK1 can act as a checkpoint in the macrophage inflammation program.
source: In addition, DAPK1 can act as a checkpoint in the macrophage inflammation program (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008) and as a negative regulator of T-cell receptor-mediated activation of NFκB (Chuang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008.

claim: DAPK1 acts as a negative regulator of T-cell receptor-mediated activation of NFκB.
source: In addition, DAPK1 can act as a checkpoint in the macrophage inflammation program (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008) and as a negative regulator of T-cell receptor-mediated activation of NFκB (Chuang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2008.

claim: C. elegans DAPK-1 plays roles in autophagy.
source: In the nematode C. elegans the sole DAPK family member, DAPK-1, plays roles in autophagy and in excitotoxic neuronal death (Del Rosario et al., 2015; Kang and Avery, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Rosario et al., 2015 and Kang and Avery, 2010.

claim: C. elegans DAPK-1 plays roles in excitotoxic neuronal death.
source: In the nematode C. elegans the sole DAPK family member, DAPK-1, plays roles in autophagy and in excitotoxic neuronal death (Del Rosario et al., 2015; Kang and Avery, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Rosario et al., 2015 and Kang and Avery, 2010.

claim: Mutations in dapk-1 result in progressive degeneration of the epidermis.
source: Mutations in dapk-1 result in progressive degeneration of the epidermis, cuticle hypertrophy, and constitutive activation of epidermal innate immune responses via a p38 MAPK cascade (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in dapk-1 result in cuticle hypertrophy.
source: Mutations in dapk-1 result in progressive degeneration of the epidermis, cuticle hypertrophy, and constitutive activation of epidermal innate immune responses via a p38 MAPK cascade (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in dapk-1 result in constitutive activation of epidermal innate immune responses via a p38 MAPK cascade.
source: Mutations in dapk-1 result in progressive degeneration of the epidermis, cuticle hypertrophy, and constitutive activation of epidermal innate immune responses via a p38 MAPK cascade (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: dapk-1 mutants exhibit faster wound repair when wounded.
source: Such dapk-1 mutants behave as if they are constitutively wounded even without injury, and when wounded exhibit faster wound repair (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: All dapk-1 mutants display epidermal morphological (Mor) defects.
source: All dapk-1 mutants display epidermal morphological (Mor) defects, with penetrance varying depending on the allele (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: The Mor phenotype reflects a progressive accumulation of the cuticle and degeneration of the underlying epidermis at the extreme anterior and posterior, as well as the dorsal midline.
source: The Mor phenotype reflects a progressive accumulation of the cuticle and degeneration of the underlying epidermis at the extreme anterior and posterior, as well as the dorsal midline.
evidence: Descriptive statement about the Mor phenotype based on observations.

claim: dapk-1(ju4) causes 100% of animals to display aberrant morphology.
source: dapk-1(ju4), which causes a missense alteration S179L in the DAPK-1 kinase domain, causes 100% of animals to display this aberrant morphology.
evidence: Stated in text and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: dapk-1(ju4) causes a missense alteration S179L in the DAPK-1 kinase domain.
source: dapk-1(ju4), which causes a missense alteration S179L in the DAPK-1 kinase domain, causes 100% of animals to display this aberrant morphology.
evidence: Molecular characterization of the ju4 allele.

claim: ptrn-1(ju698) causes a nonsense mutation in ptrn-1.
source: One suppressor, ju698, causes a nonsense mutation in ptrn-1, which encodes the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP/Nezha family of MT minus end binding proteins.
evidence: Identified through genetic suppressor screen and sequencing.

claim: ptrn-1 encodes the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP/Nezha family of MT minus end binding proteins.
source: One suppressor, ju698, causes a nonsense mutation in ptrn-1, which encodes the C. elegans member of the Patronin/CAMSAP/Nezha family of MT minus end binding proteins.
evidence: Known gene identity and function.

claim: A null allele ptrn-1(lt1) suppressed dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes to the same extent as ptrn-1(ju698).
source: A null allele ptrn-1(lt1) suppressed dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes to the same extent as ptrn-1(ju698) (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by ptrn-1(0) was rescued by a single-copy insertion (Mos-SCI) ptrn-1(+) transgene.
source: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by ptrn-1(0) was rescued by a single-copy insertion (Mos-SCI) ptrn-1(+) transgene and by transgenes expressing PTRN-1 under the control of the dpy-7 promoter, specific to the larval epidermis, indicating that loss of PTRN-1 function in the larval epidermis is required for suppression of the dapk-1(ju4) phenotype.
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment demonstrating tissue-specific requirement.

claim: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by ptrn-1(0) was rescued by transgenes expressing PTRN-1 under the control of the dpy-7 promoter.
source: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by ptrn-1(0) was rescued by a single-copy insertion (Mos-SCI) ptrn-1(+) transgene and by transgenes expressing PTRN-1 under the control of the dpy-7 promoter, specific to the larval epidermis, indicating that loss of PTRN-1 function in the larval epidermis is required for suppression of the dapk-1(ju4) phenotype.
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment demonstrating tissue-specific requirement.

claim: Loss of PTRN-1 function in the larval epidermis is required for suppression of the dapk-1(ju4) phenotype.
source: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by ptrn-1(0) was rescued by a single-copy insertion (Mos-SCI) ptrn-1(+) transgene and by transgenes expressing PTRN-1 under the control of the dpy-7 promoter, specific to the larval epidermis, indicating that loss of PTRN-1 function in the larval epidermis is required for suppression of the dapk-1(ju4) phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: dhc-1(ju697) results in a missense change G2537S in the fifth P-loop of DHC-1.
source: Our screen also identified a mutation in the dynein heavy chain, dhc-1(ju697), which results in a missense change G2537S in the fifth P-loop of DHC-1.
evidence: Molecular characterization of the ju697 allele.

claim: Complete loss of function in dhc-1 causes lethality.
source: Complete loss of function in dhc-1 causes lethality (Gonczy et al., 1999); an independent loss-of-function allele dhc-1(or195ts) fully suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects at 20°C (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonczy et al., 1999.

claim: dhc-1(or195ts) fully suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects at 20°C.
source: Complete loss of function in dhc-1 causes lethality (Gonczy et al., 1999); an independent loss-of-function allele dhc-1(or195ts) fully suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects at 20°C (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Suppression of dapk-1(ju4) by dhc-1(or195ts) was rescued by a DHC-1::GFP single-copy insertion transgene.
source: This suppression was rescued by a DHC-1::GFP single-copy insertion transgene (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PTRN-1 and other CAMSAP proteins interact with MT minus ends.
source: PTRN-1 and other CAMSAP proteins interact with MT minus ends (Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Jiang et al., 2014), and dynein is critical for MT minus-end dependent transport and MT organization.
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodwin and Vale, 2010 and Jiang et al., 2014.

claim: Dynein is critical for MT minus-end dependent transport and MT organization.
source: PTRN-1 and other CAMSAP proteins interact with MT minus ends (Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Jiang et al., 2014), and dynein is critical for MT minus-end dependent transport and MT organization.
evidence: General knowledge about dynein function.

claim: dhc-1(or195) or dhc-1(or195); ptrn-1(0) caused more complete suppression of dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes than did ptrn-1(0).
source: We found that dhc-1(or195) or dhc-1(or195); ptrn-1(0) caused more complete suppression of dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes than did ptrn-1(0), suggesting DHC-1 might affect additional pathways required for dapk-1 function.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DHC-1 might affect additional pathways required for dapk-1 function.
source: We found that dhc-1(or195) or dhc-1(or195); ptrn-1(0) caused more complete suppression of dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes than did ptrn-1(0), suggesting DHC-1 might affect additional pathways required for dapk-1 function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dhc-1 suppression is more complete than ptrn-1.

claim: ju1143 results in a nonsense mutation Q608stop in dapk-1(ju4).
source: We also isolated two intragenic suppressors, ju1143 and ju1145, which result in nonsense mutations (Q608stop and R48stop) in dapk-1(ju4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Molecular characterization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ju1145 results in a nonsense mutation R48stop in dapk-1(ju4).
source: We also isolated two intragenic suppressors, ju1143 and ju1145, which result in nonsense mutations (Q608stop and R48stop) in dapk-1(ju4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Molecular characterization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ju1143 reduces the penetrance of dapk-1(ju4) Mor phenotypes from 100% to 40%.
source: These mutations reduce the penetrance of dapk-1(ju4) Mor phenotypes from 100% to 40% and 30% respectively, and resemble the dapk-1(gk219) deletion allele and other newly generated deletions of the dapk-1 locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ju1145 reduces the penetrance of dapk-1(ju4) Mor phenotypes from 100% to 30%.
source: These mutations reduce the penetrance of dapk-1(ju4) Mor phenotypes from 100% to 40% and 30% respectively, and resemble the dapk-1(gk219) deletion allele and other newly generated deletions of the dapk-1 locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes are recessive.
source: Although dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes are recessive, the identification of such intragenic suppressors suggests ju4 causes a gain of function (see Discussion).
evidence: Stated as a known property of the allele.

claim: The identification of intragenic suppressors suggests ju4 causes a gain of function.
source: Although dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes are recessive, the identification of such intragenic suppressors suggests ju4 causes a gain of function (see Discussion).
evidence: Inferred from the genetic behavior of intragenic suppressors.

claim: ptrn-1(lt1) completely suppressed dapk-1(gk219) morphological phenotypes.
source: Both ptrn-1(lt1) and dhc-1(or195) completely suppressed dapk-1(gk219) morphological phenotypes (Figure 1B), suggesting loss of function in PTRN-1 or DHC-1 bypasses the requirement for DAPK-1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: dhc-1(or195) completely suppressed dapk-1(gk219) morphological phenotypes.
source: Both ptrn-1(lt1) and dhc-1(or195) completely suppressed dapk-1(gk219) morphological phenotypes (Figure 1B), suggesting loss of function in PTRN-1 or DHC-1 bypasses the requirement for DAPK-1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of function in PTRN-1 or DHC-1 bypasses the requirement for DAPK-1.
source: Both ptrn-1(lt1) and dhc-1(or195) completely suppressed dapk-1(gk219) morphological phenotypes (Figure 1B), suggesting loss of function in PTRN-1 or DHC-1 bypasses the requirement for DAPK-1.
evidence: Inferred from complete suppression of null allele phenotypes.

claim: Partial loss of function in unc-116 suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects.
source: Partial loss of function in unc-116, which encodes a kinesin-1 plus-end directed motor, suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects.
evidence: Shown in Table 1 and Figure 1B.

claim: unc-116 encodes a kinesin-1 plus-end directed motor.
source: Partial loss of function in unc-116, which encodes a kinesin-1 plus-end directed motor, suppressed dapk-1(ju4) morphological defects.
evidence: Known gene identity.

claim: DAPK family members have previously been implicated in MT stability, promoting function of the MT-associated protein tau via the Pin1 prolyl isomerase or the MARK kinase.
source: DAPK family members have previously been implicated in MT stability, promoting function of the MT-associated protein tau via the Pin1 prolyl isomerase or the MARK kinase (Kim et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2014 and Wu et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of function in orthologs of Pin1, pinn-1, and MARK/par-1 did not modify dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes.
source: However, loss of function in orthologs of these genes (ptl-1, pinn-1, par-1) did not modify dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes (Table 1), suggesting DAPK-1 regulates epidermal MTs via a novel mechanism.
evidence: Shown in Table 1.

claim: DAPK-1 regulates epidermal MTs via a novel mechanism.
source: However, loss of function in orthologs of these genes (ptl-1, pinn-1, par-1) did not modify dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes (Table 1), suggesting DAPK-1 regulates epidermal MTs via a novel mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from lack of genetic interaction with known DAPK-tau pathway components.

claim: dapk-1 mutants display accelerated epidermal wound closure.
source: dapk-1 mutants also display accelerated epidermal wound closure, manifested by the rate of closure of actin rings that form around puncture wounds (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: ptrn-1 mutations suppressed the accelerated wound closure of dapk-1 mutants to wild type rates.
source: We found that ptrn-1 mutations suppressed this accelerated wound closure to wild type rates (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ptrn-1(0) single mutants displayed significantly delayed wound closure compared to the wild type.
source: Moreover, ptrn-1(0) single mutants displayed significantly delayed wound closure compared to the wild type.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: DAPK-1 and PTRN-1 play antagonistic roles in epidermal development and in wound repair.
source: Thus, DAPK-1 and PTRN-1 play antagonistic roles in epidermal development and in wound repair.
evidence: Inferred from opposing effects on wound closure and morphology.

claim: CAMSAPs are thought to promote MT stability in part by protecting minus ends from the MT depolymerizing enzyme kinesin-13.
source: CAMSAPs are thought to promote MT stability in part by protecting minus ends from the MT depolymerizing enzyme kinesin-13 (Goodwin and Vale, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goodwin and Vale, 2010.

claim: Loss of function in klp-7/kinesin-13 strongly enhanced morphological defects of dapk-1(gk219).
source: Consistent with this model, loss of function in klp-7/kinesin-13 strongly enhanced morphological defects of dapk-1(gk219), both in ptrn-1(+) and in ptrn-1(0) backgrounds (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Partial loss of function of MEI-1/p60 katanin enhanced dapk-1(gk219) Mor phenotypes.
source: Partial loss of function of the MT severing enzymes MEI-1/p60 katanin or SPAS-1/Spastin also enhanced dapk-1(gk219) Mor phenotypes.
evidence: Shown in Table 1.

claim: Partial loss of function of SPAS-1/Spastin enhanced dapk-1(gk219) Mor phenotypes.
source: Partial loss of function of the MT severing enzymes MEI-1/p60 katanin or SPAS-1/Spastin also enhanced dapk-1(gk219) Mor phenotypes.
evidence: Shown in Table 1.

claim: klp-7, mei-1, and spas-1 mutants did not confer morphological defects in a dapk-1(+) background.
source: None of these mutants conferred morphological defects in a dapk-1(+) background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Aberrant dapk-1 function causes epidermal integrity to be sensitized to MT stability.
source: These analyses suggest that aberrant dapk-1 function causes epidermal integrity to be sensitized to MT stability.
evidence: Inferred from genetic interactions with MT regulators.

claim: dapk-1(ju4) animals constitutively express high levels of AMPs such as nlp-29 and nlp-30.
source: dapk-1(ju4) animals constitutively express high levels of AMPs such as nlp-29 and nlp-30, and this hyperactive epidermal immune response is genetically separable from dapk-1(ju4) epidermal morphological defects (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: The hyperactive epidermal immune response in dapk-1(ju4) is genetically separable from dapk-1(ju4) epidermal morphological defects.
source: dapk-1(ju4) animals constitutively express high levels of AMPs such as nlp-29 and nlp-30, and this hyperactive epidermal immune response is genetically separable from dapk-1(ju4) epidermal morphological defects (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: dhc-1(or195) did not suppress the elevated innate immune response in dapk-1(ju4).
source: Neither mutant suppressed the elevated innate immune response in dapk-1(ju4) (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), as measured using a Pnlp-29-GFP transcriptional reporter.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: unc-116(e2310) did not suppress the elevated innate immune response in dapk-1(ju4).
source: Neither mutant suppressed the elevated innate immune response in dapk-1(ju4) (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), as measured using a Pnlp-29-GFP transcriptional reporter.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ptrn-1(0) fully suppressed the elevated immune response of dapk-1(ju4).
source: In contrast, ptrn-1(0) fully suppressed the elevated immune response of dapk-1(ju4) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: DAPK-1 acts in the epidermis to maintain epidermal morphology.
source: DAPK-1 acts in the epidermis to maintain epidermal morphology (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: Epidermal development is overtly normal in ptrn-1(0) mutants.
source: Although epidermal development is overtly normal in ptrn-1(0) mutants, PTRN-1 acts redundantly with γ-tubulin and the ninein-like protein NOCA-1 to assemble noncentrosomal MT arrays essential for epidermal development (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Observation and citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: PTRN-1 acts redundantly with γ-tubulin and the ninein-like protein NOCA-1 to assemble noncentrosomal MT arrays essential for epidermal development.
source: Although epidermal development is overtly normal in ptrn-1(0) mutants, PTRN-1 acts redundantly with γ-tubulin and the ninein-like protein NOCA-1 to assemble noncentrosomal MT arrays essential for epidermal development (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of function in γ-tubulin/TBG-1 did not suppress dapk-1(ju4) epidermal defects.
source: However, loss of function in γ-tubulin/TBG-1 did not suppress dapk-1(ju4) epidermal defects (Table 1), suggesting DAPK-1 specifically interacts with the PTRN-1 pathway.
evidence: Shown in Table 1.

claim: DAPK-1 specifically interacts with the PTRN-1 pathway.
source: However, loss of function in γ-tubulin/TBG-1 did not suppress dapk-1(ju4) epidermal defects (Table 1), suggesting DAPK-1 specifically interacts with the PTRN-1 pathway.
evidence: Inferred from lack of suppression by tbg-1 but suppression by ptrn-1.

claim: ptrn-1 mutations suppressed the accelerated wound closure of dapk-1 mutants.
source: We found that ptrn-1 mutations suppressed this accelerated wound closure to wild type rates (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Colchicine treatment significantly suppressed the epidermal morphology defects of dapk-1(gk219) animals.
source: Colchicine treatment significantly suppressed the epidermal morphology defects of dapk-1(gk219) animals (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A.

claim: cat-4 strongly enhanced dapk-1(gk219).
source: cat-4 itself strongly enhanced dapk-1(gk219), suggesting that dapk-1 is also sensitized to defects in cuticle integrity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dapk-1 is sensitized to defects in cuticle integrity.
source: cat-4 itself strongly enhanced dapk-1(gk219), suggesting that dapk-1 is also sensitized to defects in cuticle integrity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from enhancement by cat-4, which has leaky cuticles.

claim: The morphological defects of dapk-1(gk219) cat-4 animals were suppressed by colchicine in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The morphological defects of dapk-1(gk219) cat-4 animals were suppressed by colchicine in a dose-dependent manner, and high concentrations of colchicine (5 mM) significantly suppressed dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High concentrations of colchicine (5 mM) significantly suppressed dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes.
source: The morphological defects of dapk-1(gk219) cat-4 animals were suppressed by colchicine in a dose-dependent manner, and high concentrations of colchicine (5 mM) significantly suppressed dapk-1(ju4) phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with paclitaxel enhanced dapk-1(gk219) morphological defects.
source: Conversely, treatment with the MT stabilizing drug paclitaxel enhanced dapk-1(gk219) morphological defects, consistent with Mor phenotypes in dapk-1(ju4) mutants being caused by hyper-stabilized MTs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mor phenotypes in dapk-1(ju4) mutants are caused by hyper-stabilized MTs.
source: Conversely, treatment with the MT stabilizing drug paclitaxel enhanced dapk-1(gk219) morphological defects, consistent with Mor phenotypes in dapk-1(ju4) mutants being caused by hyper-stabilized MTs (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from enhancement by MT-stabilizing drug and suppression by MT-destabilizing drug.

claim: Paclitaxel treatment of wild type animals could induce dapk-1-like epidermal defects, albeit at very low penetrance.
source: Indeed, paclitaxel treatment of wild type animals could induce dapk-1-like epidermal defects, albeit at very low penetrance (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: ptrn-1(0) mutants were six times more sensitive to the effects of paclitaxel compared to WT animals.
source: ptrn-1(0) mutants display overtly normal epidermal morphology, but were six times more sensitive to the effects of paclitaxel compared to WT animals (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Paclitaxel induced morphological defects in dapk-1(gk219) ptrn-1(0) double mutants.
source: Paclitaxel also induced morphological defects in dapk-1(gk219) ptrn-1(0) double mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), although not to the same extent as in dapk-1(gk219) single mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dhc-1(or195) single mutants were hypersensitive to paclitaxel, compared to wild type.
source: dhc-1(or195) single mutants were also hypersensitive to paclitaxel, compared to wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), possibly reflecting increased free tubulin concentration in these mutants.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Increased free tubulin concentration in dhc-1(or195) mutants may explain their hypersensitivity to paclitaxel.
source: dhc-1(or195) single mutants were also hypersensitive to paclitaxel, compared to wild type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), possibly reflecting increased free tubulin concentration in these mutants.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed hypersensitivity.

claim: At high concentrations of colchicine there was significant suppression of dapk-1(ju4) innate immune responses.

claim: GFP::DAPK-1 puncta aggregated in the anterior epidermis, where morphological defects were prominent.
source: GFP::DAPK-1 puncta also aggregated at the edges of the epidermal ridges along the body (Figure 7A), as well as in the anterior epidermis, where morphological defects were prominent (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the lateral epidermis GFP::DAPK-1 puncta moved at 1.33 ± 0.028 µm/s.
source: In the lateral epidermis GFP::DAPK-1 puncta moved at 1.33 ± 0.028 µm/s; GFP::DAPK-1 movement in the dorsoventral epidermis was slightly slower (Table 3).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Table 3.

claim: GFP::DAPK-1 movement in the dorsoventral epidermis was slightly slower than in the lateral epidermis.
source: In the lateral epidermis GFP::DAPK-1 puncta moved at 1.33 ± 0.028 µm/s; GFP::DAPK-1 movement in the dorsoventral epidermis was slightly slower (Table 3).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Table 3.

claim: Colchicine treatment severely reduced the number of moving GFP::DAPK-1 puncta.
source: Colchicine treatment severely reduced the number of moving GFP::DAPK-1 puncta (Figure 7E); movement of the remaining puncta was slightly slowed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Colchicine treatment slightly slowed the movement of the remaining GFP::DAPK-1 puncta.
source: Colchicine treatment severely reduced the number of moving GFP::DAPK-1 puncta (Figure 7E); movement of the remaining puncta was slightly slowed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP::DAPK-1 puncta moved ~5 times faster than EBP-2::GFP comets.
source: GFP::DAPK-1 puncta moved ~5 times faster than EBP-2::GFP comets (Figure 7F; Table 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7F and Table 3.

claim: In contrast to the unidirectional movement of GFP::DAPK-1 away from epidermal ridges, plus-end growth occurred in both directions in the dorsoventral epidermis.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the unidirectional movement of GFP::DAPK-1 away from epidermal ridges plus-end growth occurred in both directions in the dorsoventral epidermis (Figure 7G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7G.

claim: GFP::DAPK-1 dynamics reflect MT-based transport.
source: We infer that GFP::DAPK-1 dynamics reflect MT-based transport.
evidence: Inferred from MT-dependence and velocity of movement.

claim: Both GFP::DAPK-1(ΔKinase) and GFP::DAPK-1(S179L) formed dynamic puncta that moved at normal or slightly slower velocities.
source: Both GFP::DAPK-1(ΔKinase) and GFP::DAPK-1(S179L) formed dynamic puncta that moved at normal or slightly slower velocities (Table 4; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown in Table 4 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP::DAPK-1 lacking either the cytoskeletal binding domain or the death domain did not form puncta.
source: Conversely GFP::DAPK-1 lacking either the cytoskeletal binding domain or the death domain did not form puncta (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No single domain was sufficient for the formation of motile puncta.
source: No single domain was sufficient for the formation of motile puncta (Table 4).
evidence: Shown in Table 4.

claim: The kinase domain, ankyrin domain, and cytoskeleton-binding domain by themselves occasionally formed stationary puncta.
source: However, the kinase domain, ankyrin domain, and cytoskeleton-binding domain by themselves occasionally formed stationary puncta (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Multiple non-kinase domains are required for formation of motile DAPK-1 puncta.
source: In summary, multiple non-kinase domains are required for formation of motile DAPK-1 puncta; formation of motile puncta could be necessary but not sufficient for DAPK-1 function.
evidence: Inferred from domain deletion analysis.

claim: Formation of motile puncta could be necessary but not sufficient for DAPK-1 function.
source: In summary, multiple non-kinase domains are required for formation of motile DAPK-1 puncta; formation of motile puncta could be necessary but not sufficient for DAPK-1 function.
evidence: Inferred from structure-function analysis.

claim: The velocity of DAPK-1 puncta did not change in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants.
source: The velocity of DAPK-1 puncta did not change in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants, but decreased two-fold in dhc-1(or195) mutants (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The velocity of DAPK-1 puncta decreased two-fold in dhc-1(or195) mutants.
source: The velocity of DAPK-1 puncta did not change in unc-116/kinesin-1 mutants, but decreased two-fold in dhc-1(or195) mutants (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7H.

claim: ptrn-1(0) mutants had fewer moving DAPK-1 puncta in the dorsoventral epidermis.
source: ptrn-1(0) mutants had fewer moving DAPK-1 puncta in the dorsoventral epidermis, consistent with their reduced numbers of circumferential MTs (Figure 7I); the velocity of the remaining GFP::DAPK-1 puncta was normal.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The velocity of the remaining GFP::DAPK-1 puncta in ptrn-1(0) mutants was normal.
source: ptrn-1(0) mutants had fewer moving DAPK-1 puncta in the dorsoventral epidermis, consistent with their reduced numbers of circumferential MTs (Figure 7I); the velocity of the remaining GFP::DAPK-1 puncta was normal.
evidence: Stated in text.

claim: Neither ptrn-1(0) nor dhc-1 mutants affected the directional bias of GFP::DAPK-1 transport.
source: Neither ptrn-1(0) nor dhc-1 mutants affected the directional bias of GFP::DAPK-1 transport (Figure 7J).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7J.

claim: dapk-1(ju4) is a gain of function mutation.
source: This allele, unlike dapk-1(gk219) or deletions of the dapk-1 locus, causes fully penetrant morphological phenotypes. Our identification of stop codon mutations as intragenic revertants, as well as the finding that transgenic expression of S179L DAPK-1 induces Mor phenotypes, suggests dapk-1(ju4) is a gain of function mutation.
evidence: Inferred from intragenic suppressors and transgenic expression.

claim: The S179L change may alter the phosphorylation specificity of DAPK-1.
source: One hypothesis for why dapk-1(ju4) has a more penetrant effect on epidermal morphology than the complete loss of dapk-1 function is that the S179L change alters the phosphorylation specificity of DAPK-1.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis to explain gain of function.

claim: DAPK-1(Δkinase) strongly enhanced, but did not induce, dapk-1 phenotypes.
source: In our assays, DAPK-1(Δkinase) strongly enhanced, but did not induce, dapk-1 phenotypes, while DAPK-1(kinase dead) did neither.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DAPK-1(kinase dead) did not enhance or induce dapk-1 phenotypes.
source: In our assays, DAPK-1(Δkinase) strongly enhanced, but did not induce, dapk-1 phenotypes, while DAPK-1(kinase dead) did neither.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DAPK-1(S179L) is unlikely to be kinase-dead.
source: Thus, DAPK-1(S179L) is unlikely to be kinase-dead, but may have an aberrantly regulated kinase activity.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with kinase-dead mutant.

claim: DAPK-1(S179L) may have an aberrantly regulated kinase activity.
source: Thus, DAPK-1(S179L) is unlikely to be kinase-dead, but may have an aberrantly regulated kinase activity.
evidence: Speculative explanation for gain of function.

claim: DAPK-1's normal function is to restrain epidermal MT stabilization.
source: Our pharmacological data suggest DAPK-1's normal function is to restrain epidermal MT stabilization.
evidence: Inferred from drug treatment experiments.

claim: DAPK-1 may be regulating epidermal MT stability at least partially through PTRN-1.
source: Our suppressor screen and tests of candidate genes suggests a specific interaction between ptrn-1 and dapk-1; thus, DAPK-1 may be regulating epidermal MT stability at least partially through PTRN-1.
evidence: Inferred from specific genetic interactions.

claim: Epidermal morphology is more sensitive to MT disruption than is the innate immune response.
source: Our analysis using MT drugs shows that the concentrations of drugs sufficient to suppress or induce morphological defects are insufficient to suppress or induce innate immune responses, consistent with previous observations (Zhang et al., 2015). Thus, epidermal morphology is more sensitive to MT disruption than is the innate immune response, and MT stabilization may affect innate immune responses indirectly via effects on epidermal integrity.
evidence: Inferred from differential drug sensitivity of morphology vs. immunity.

claim: MT stabilization may affect innate immune responses indirectly via effects on epidermal integrity.
source: Our analysis using MT drugs shows that the concentrations of drugs sufficient to suppress or induce morphological defects are insufficient to suppress or induce innate immune responses, consistent with previous observations (Zhang et al., 2015). Thus, epidermal morphology is more sensitive to MT disruption than is the innate immune response, and MT stabilization may affect innate immune responses indirectly via effects on epidermal integrity.
evidence: Inferred from drug effects on morphology and immunity.

claim: During postembryonic development the epidermis becomes more dependent on PTRN-1 and on noncentrosomal MT arrays.
source: Thus during postembryonic development the epidermis becomes more dependent on PTRN-1 and on noncentrosomal MT arrays.
evidence: Inferred from worsening ptrn-1 phenotype in adults vs. larvae.

claim: The requirement for PTRN-1 in repair but not in development may reflect the prominent role of noncentrosomal MT arrays in mature neurons and epithelia.
source: The requirement for PTRN-1 in repair but not in development may reflect the prominent role of noncentrosomal MT arrays in mature neurons and epithelia.
evidence: Speculative explanation for developmental stage-specific requirement.

claim: The CKK domain can target MT minus ends, or can bind along the lattice depending on the particular CAMSAP family member.
source: Depending on the particular CAMSAP family member, the CKK domain can target MT minus ends, or can bind along the lattice (Goodwin and Vale, 2010; Jiang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodwin and Vale, 2010 and Jiang et al., 2014.

claim: In C. elegans PTRN-1 requires the CKK domain to localize to MTs in neurons and muscles.
source: In C. elegans PTRN-1 requires the CKK domain to localize to MTs in neurons and muscles (Richardson et al., 2014), and the CKK domain can stabilize neuronal MTs (Chuang et al., 2014), consistent with MT stability being a determinant of epidermal morphology.
evidence: Supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2014.

claim: The CKK domain can stabilize neuronal MTs.
source: In C. elegans PTRN-1 requires the CKK domain to localize to MTs in neurons and muscles (Richardson et al., 2014), and the CKK domain can stabilize neuronal MTs (Chuang et al., 2014), consistent with MT stability being a determinant of epidermal morphology.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2014.

claim: MT stability is a determinant of epidermal morphology.
source: In C. elegans PTRN-1 requires the CKK domain to localize to MTs in neurons and muscles (Richardson et al., 2014), and the CKK domain can stabilize neuronal MTs (Chuang et al., 2014), consistent with MT stability being a determinant of epidermal morphology.
evidence: Inferred from CKK domain effects on MTs and morphology.

claim: DAPK-1 might directly or indirectly inhibit CKK activity.
source: Little is known about how CKK domain activity is regulated, but our data suggest DAPK-1 might directly or indirectly inhibit CKK activity; moreover, the CH or CC domains of PTRN-1 appear to inhibit CKK activity.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and biochemical interactions.

claim: The CH or CC domains of PTRN-1 appear to inhibit CKK activity.
source: Little is known about how CKK domain activity is regulated, but our data suggest DAPK-1 might directly or indirectly inhibit CKK activity; moreover, the CH or CC domains of PTRN-1 appear to inhibit CKK activity.
evidence: Inferred from domain deletion experiments.

claim: In the absence of the CC domain, ectopic association of the CKK domain along the MT lattice (long thin filaments) results in aberrant MT stabilization.
source: As the CC domain of PTRN-1 appears to target to minus ends, a possible mechanism is that in the absence of the CC domain, ectopic association of the CKK domain along the MT lattice (long thin filaments) results in aberrant MT stabilization.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on localization patterns.

claim: DAPK-1 might inhibit the activity of the CKK domain indirectly via the CC or CH domains.
source: DAPK-1 might inhibit the activity of the CKK domain indirectly via the CC or CH domains (Figure 8).
evidence: Speculative model shown in Figure 8.

claim: DAPK family members have not been previously shown to undergo MT-dependent transport.
source: To our knowledge, DAPK family members have not been previously shown to undergo MT-dependent transport.
evidence: Statement about novelty of finding.

claim: In the C. elegans epidermis the MT cytoskeleton is required for cell shape changes.
source: In the C. elegans epidermis the MT cytoskeleton is required for cell shape changes (Priess and Hirsh, 1986; Quintin et al., 2016) and for nuclear migrations (Starr, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Priess and Hirsh, 1986 and Quintin et al., 2016.

claim: In the C. elegans epidermis the MT cytoskeleton is required for nuclear migrations.
source: In the C. elegans epidermis the MT cytoskeleton is required for cell shape changes (Priess and Hirsh, 1986; Quintin et al., 2016) and for nuclear migrations (Starr, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Starr, 2011.

claim: Epidermal MTs are critical for larval development.
source: Epidermal MTs are critical for larval development: noncentrosomal arrays of the larval epidermis require PTRN-1 and the NOCA-1/γ-tubulin pathway (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Noncentrosomal arrays of the larval epidermis require PTRN-1 and the NOCA-1/γ-tubulin pathway.
source: Epidermal MTs are critical for larval development: noncentrosomal arrays of the larval epidermis require PTRN-1 and the NOCA-1/γ-tubulin pathway (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: In the context of dapk-1 epidermal defects, PTRN-1 and NOCA-1 pathways are not equivalent.
source: In contrast, PTRN-1 is required non-redundantly for dapk-1 epidermal defects, suggesting that in this context PTRN-1 and NOCA-1 pathways are not equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from lack of suppression by tbg-1 but suppression by ptrn-1.

claim: As the epidermis grows during larval development and adult life, it may become increasingly dependent on intracellular transport.
source: We speculate that the architecture of the epidermis may make it increasingly dependent on intracellular transport as it grows during larval development and adult life.
evidence: Speculative explanation for developmental stage-specific effects.

claim: Epidermal nuclei are confined to lateral and ventral ridges.
source: Epidermal nuclei are confined to lateral and ventral ridges.
evidence: Known anatomical feature of C. elegans epidermis.

claim: The squamified dorsoventral epidermis is a barrier to diffusion.
source: The squamified dorsoventral epidermis is a barrier to diffusion.
evidence: Inferred from thin structure of dorsoventral epidermis.

claim: As in neuronal axons, extensive intracellular transport may be required to supply distant regions of the cell with cellular constituents.
source: Thus, as in neuronal axons, extensive intracellular transport may be required to supply distant regions of the cell with cellular constituents.
evidence: Speculative analogy to neurons.

claim: DAPK-1 may maintain MT dynamics required for active transport of materials to the remoter areas of the epidermis.
source: DAPK-1 may maintain MT dynamics required for active transport of materials to the remoter areas of the epidermis.
evidence: Speculative model for DAPK-1 function.

claim: The loss of dapk-1 function has a stronger effect on MT architecture in the lateral epidermis compared to the dorsoventral epidermis.
source: Furthermore, our data show that the loss of dapk-1 function has a stronger effect on MT architecture in the lateral epidermis compared to the dorsoventral epidermis, perhaps due to differences in the local MTOCs or PTRN-1 in these different compartments.
evidence: Shown in MT architecture analysis.

claim: Differences in MT architecture effects between lateral and dorsoventral epidermis may be due to differences in the local MTOCs or PTRN-1 in these different compartments.
source: Furthermore, our data show that the loss of dapk-1 function has a stronger effect on MT architecture in the lateral epidermis compared to the dorsoventral epidermis, perhaps due to differences in the local MTOCs or PTRN-1 in these different compartments.
evidence: Speculative explanation for compartment-specific effects.
